name: Northeast Buttress ("Come Over to the Dark Side")
rappels: No published count. The descent is a full day of rappelling back down the line of ascent - through the upper north face and the north/northeast buttress system - and no bolts were drilled on the route, so every anchor is built and left behind. Carry extra cord and tat for it, and plan retreat before committing to the upper wall: above the midpoint, complex routefinding and sparse anchors make it slow.
descent_text: The first-ascent party descended by rappelling back down through the upper north face and the north/northeast buttress system over the course of a day, retracing the general line of ascent to their camp below the wall.
approach: A roughly two-day approach traveling via the remnants of the McMillan Creek glaciers to reach the base of the peak's north side/northeast buttress; on the day of the climb the party hiked about 3.5 hours from a high camp to the base of the wall.
overview: A long, sustained new-wave buttress route up East McMillan Spire's dramatic 2,400-foot northeast wall, climbing compact Skagit gneiss on mostly moderate (5.6-5.8) rock with a handful of 5.9 pitches and three or four pitches of 5.10-.
beta: Established over 3 days in September 2008 by Alan Kearney and Erik Johnson (a route Kearney had attempted in 1991 and 2003), the line follows the peak's northeast buttress up compact gneiss with few natural crack systems. The pair placed small cams and numerous knifeblade and bugaboo pitons for protection and drilled no bolts; the route is described as featuring dark, brooding overhangs, a delicate traverse, sections of blank rock, and loose, teetering blocks near the top.
